event: My manager cancelled our 1:1 meeting 30 minutes before it started.
rawInterpretation: My manager is losing interest in supporting me and probably thinks I am not performing well.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers often reschedule due to competing priorities.
A cancelled meeting does not necessarily reflect the value of the employee.
Performance concerns are usually communicated more directly.
There is no evidence that the cancellation is related to your performance.
revisedInterpretation: I feel disappointed, but a cancelled meeting alone does not indicate dissatisfaction with my work.
chosenBehaviour: Wait for the rescheduled meeting and avoid making assumptions.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager rescheduled the meeting and discussed project priorities.

event: A colleague challenged my proposal during a team meeting.
rawInterpretation: They were trying to undermine me in front of everyone.
alternateRealityChecks: The challenge may have been directed at the idea rather than you.
Healthy disagreement is common in decision making.
Questions often help strengthen proposals.
There is insufficient evidence that the intent was personal.
revisedInterpretation: The discussion may have focused on improving the proposal rather than attacking me.
chosenBehaviour: Follow up with curiosity instead of defensiveness.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The colleague later supported an updated version of the proposal.

event: Nobody responded to my Teams message for several hours.
rawInterpretation: The team does not value my input.
alternateRealityChecks: People may have been in meetings.
Some questions require more thought before responding.
Response speed does not equal respect.
Others may not have considered the message urgent.
revisedInterpretation: The lack of immediate replies is not sufficient evidence that my input is undervalued.
chosenBehaviour: Wait and send a polite follow-up if needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Several teammates replied and provided useful feedback.

event: A coworker received recognition for a project I also contributed to.
rawInterpretation: Management notices only their work and ignores mine.
alternateRealityChecks: Recognition of one person does not negate your contribution.
Managers may not have full visibility into everyone's work.
Your impact may be recognized at another opportunity.
One event does not establish a pattern.
revisedInterpretation: Recognition may have reflected visibility rather than deliberate exclusion.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager acknowledged contributions and included them in a project update.

event: My manager gave me critical feedback on a presentation.
alternateRealityChecks: Feedback often focuses on improvement opportunities.
Receiving feedback suggests investment in your growth.
One weakness does not invalidate the entire presentation.
Most professionals improve through feedback.
revisedInterpretation: The feedback is an opportunity to improve rather than proof of failure.
chosenBehaviour: Incorporate the feedback into the next presentation.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The next presentation received positive feedback.

event: A colleague stopped inviting me to informal discussions.
rawInterpretation: They no longer want to work with me.
alternateRealityChecks: The discussions may have become project specific.
The colleague may assume you already know the information.
The participant list may have changed.
There is not enough information to conclude exclusion.
revisedInterpretation: I need more context before assuming rejection.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The colleague explained the discussions involved a different project.

event: My proposal was not selected during planning.
alternateRealityChecks: Priorities depend on timing and resources.
A rejected proposal can still be valuable.
Many good ideas are postponed.
One decision does not define your credibility.
revisedInterpretation: The proposal may not have fit current priorities.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Parts of the proposal were included in the next planning cycle.

event: A senior stakeholder seemed disengaged during my presentation.
alternateRealityChecks: They may have been distracted by unrelated issues.
Different people process information differently.
Body language is not always a reliable indicator.
You have not received explicit negative feedback.
revisedInterpretation: I cannot infer their opinion solely from their behaviour.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Stakeholder provided constructive and positive comments.

event: My pull request received many review comments.
alternateRealityChecks: Comments often improve quality.
Complex work usually receives more feedback.
Code reviews are collaborative by design.
Experienced engineers also receive comments.
revisedInterpretation: The comments are part of the development process.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The PR was approved and merged.

event: A coworker interrupted me several times during a discussion.
alternateRealityChecks: Some communication styles are naturally more interruptive.
They may have been excited about the topic.
The interruptions may have been unintentional.
Intent cannot be determined from behaviour alone.
revisedInterpretation: The interruptions were frustrating but not necessarily disrespectful.
chosenBehaviour: Discuss meeting dynamics calmly if the pattern continues.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The colleague apologized and became more conscious in discussions.

event: A project decision was made without consulting me.
rawInterpretation: My expertise is no longer valued.
alternateRealityChecks: The decision may have been time sensitive.
The team may not have realized your input was needed.
The scope may have changed.
One event does not define your organisational value.
revisedInterpretation: I need more context before concluding that my expertise is undervalued.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager clarified the decision timeline and invited participation in future reviews.

event: I saw colleagues talking quietly after a meeting.
alternateRealityChecks: They may have been discussing another topic.
People often continue conversations after meetings.
There is no evidence the conversation involved you.
Assumptions are not facts.
revisedInterpretation: I do not know what they were discussing.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The discussion turned out to be about a separate customer issue.

event: A teammate strongly disagreed with my recommendation.
alternateRealityChecks: People can disagree without questioning competence.
Strong opinions often occur around important decisions.
The disagreement may be about trade-offs.
Debate can improve outcomes.
revisedInterpretation: The discussion may have been focused on the recommendation rather than me.
chosenBehaviour: Explore the rationale behind the disagreement.
outcomeOneWeekLater: The team created a combined solution using ideas from both sides.

event: My promotion did not happen this cycle.
rawInterpretation: The organisation does not appreciate my work.
alternateRealityChecks: Promotion decisions consider multiple factors.
Budget and timing can influence promotions.
Performance is only one variable.
No promotion is not the same as no appreciation.
revisedInterpretation: I am disappointed, but I need more information before drawing conclusions.
chosenBehaviour: Request development feedback and promotion expectations.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager outlined a growth plan and upcoming opportunities.

event: My manager asked detailed questions about my work.
alternateRealityChecks: Managers need visibility into project status.
Questions can indicate engagement and interest.
Clarification is a normal leadership activity.
You have not received any indication of concern.
revisedInterpretation: The questions may simply be part of responsible project oversight.
chosenBehaviour: Answer factually and ask if additional details are needed.
outcomeOneWeekLater: Manager used the information to support project planning.
